TITLE: End-to-End Joint Reconstruction and Segmentation Model
PROPOSAL: We develop a novel neural network architecture, called HydraForests, that jointly predicts a human 3D mesh and segmentations from a single input image. HydraForests employs a cascaded variant of the U-Net architecture for both image-to-3D mesh reconstruction and 2D image segmentation, where 3D information is injected as skip connections to enhance realism and segmentation accuracy. A multi-scale transform is also introduced to aggregate both point-wise and structural 3D cues. By concurrently optimizing for reconstruction and segmentation, HydraForests can leverage cross-entropy and Chamfer L1 distance as joint objectives, which accelerate learning and lead to consistent results across viewpoints.
CONTROLS: We provide baselines that include state-of-the-art appearance-based 3D mesh reconstruction models (e.g. OMNIGraph) and simple 2D segmentation models using powerful 2D human foundation models (e.g., HRNet). Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are used for 3D mesh deformation to facilitate learning such as synthetic-to-real discrepancy.
COST: Estimated to be 1500 GPU hours for training the HydraForests model on the SHREC 2020 dataset and validating on e.g., the NR20-Benchmark dataset.
PREDICTION: HydraForests is expected to outperform both single-task models in terms of qualitative results and reach state-of-the-art performance on certain segmentation metrics, despite being limited to using only a single input image; however, achieving comparable Chamfer L1 distance results for novel view synthesis might be challenging due to 3D mesh loss, positing an area for future research on improved objective functions.

TITLE: Simplified Pairwise Objective Function for Chamfer L1 Distance Robustness
PROPOSAL: We introduce a simplified pairwise objective function, referred to as Pairwise-MMD, to improve the robustness of the Chamfer L1 distance. Specifically, we adapt the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) metric to compare the mesh reconstruction and the ground truth. The pairwise objective function is defined as the squared difference between the two MMD distances, which learns distances that are optimal for the given classes of the meshes. The Pairwise-MMD objective can be minimized by training the classical Chamfer L1 distance combined with the MMD term on the same training data. 
CONTROLS: We compare the new Pairwise-MMD objective to both the original Chamfer L1 distance and the existing HydraForests model with the original Chamfer L1 distance.
COST: Estimated to be an additional 15 GPU hours for training on a moderately large dataset.
PREDICTION: We expect the Pairwise-MMD objective function to outperform the Chamfer L1 distance on the symmetry and realism metrics of 3D mesh reconstruction when using the original HydraForests model. In addition, we predict that HydraForests using Pairwise-MMD can match the performance of state-of-the-art methods on these metrics and can provide more accurate results for novel view-synthesis.

PROPOSAL: We propose a comprehensive quantitative evaluation framework and visualization toolkit to assess the performance of HydraForests on 3D human reconstruction tasks. By visualizing the reconstructed meshes and comparing them to the ground truth, we provide a clear and interactive understanding of the model's strengths and weaknesses.

PROPOSAL: We present a real-world deployment of HydraForests in a user-facing application, where we integrate the model into an immersive storytelling platform for VR/AR content creation. We conduct a user study to evaluate the effectiveness of HydraForests in supporting content creators and analyze the perceived quality and usability of the system. The study focuses on identifying pain points, areas for improvement, and potential applications of the technology. Additionally, we investigate the potential for transfer learning to other domains, such as medical or educational applications, where 3D human reconstruction and segmentation can be beneficial.

TITLE: Multimodal Investigation of 3D Human Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: Investigate a multimodal approach to 3D human reconstruction by fusing information from RGB images and 2D human pose estimates, exploring the benefits of jointly training appearance, pose, and segmentation prediction tasks in a single meta-decoder architecture. We will leverage the strengths of each modality to improve the resilience and accuracy of 3D reconstruction across diverse scenarios and evaluate the impact of different fusion strategies on performance.
CONTROLS: The performance of the multimodal approach will be compared with state-of-the-art RGB-only and 2D pose-only baselines, as well as an ablation study on the efficacy of different pose representation (e.g., cartesian, spherical, and hybrid).
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the multimodal approach will lead to improved 3D reconstruction accuracy and robustness due to the fusion of complementary information from RGB images and 2D pose estimates, particularly in scenarios with occlusions, varying lighting conditions, or complex poses. However, this approach might also increase computational complexity and require larger training datasets to accommodate the additional modality.
